subject: physics_2
question_text: State Kirchhoff's laws for an electrical network. Using these laws deduce the condition for balancing in a Wheatstone bridge?

verification.note: The 2+2+2+2 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Paper-II bank the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Transcription (book p29, LAQ 1): the book prints 'State kirchoff's law for an electrical network using these laws deduce the condition for balancing in a wheatstone bridge ?'. Corrected here: the misspelling kirchoff to Kirchhoff, the dropped s in 'law' (the same sentence says 'these laws'), the proper nouns Kirchhoff and Wheatstone capitalised, a full stop added after 'network' where the printed sentence runs on, and the space before the question mark dropped. NOTATION: the galvanometer current is written i₅ here, not the book's i_g, because Unicode has no subscript g and this bank writes all on-page mathematics in real Unicode; G still means the galvanometer resistance, as in the book. Hand-checked: junction rule at C and D plus the loop rule for ACDA and CBDC give, at i₅ = 0, i₁ = i₃, i₂ = i₄, i₁P = i₂R and i₃Q = i₄S, so P/Q = R/S.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: Kirchhoff's current law
lines: Kirchhoff's first law (junction rule):
the sum of the currents entering a junction
is equal to the sum of the currents leaving
it. In other words, the algebraic sum of the
currents meeting at a junction is zero.
For the junction drawn below,
This law follows from the conservation of
charge.
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Statement, the equation, and the conservation law it rests on.
steps.why: Charge does not collect at a junction, because a junction is only a meeting point of wires with no capacity to store charge. Whatever charge arrives each second must leave each second, and that is the junction rule.
common_mistakes: Naming the wrong conservation law. The junction rule is charge; the loop rule is energy.
Writing the sums without saying which currents enter and which leave.

recall.must_convey: That the current entering a junction equals the current leaving it, and that this follows from conservation of charge.
accept: sum of currents entering equals sum leaving
algebraic sum of currents at a junction is zero
reject: sum of potential differences is zero

steps.memory_tip: Junction rule goes with charge; loop rule goes with energy.

steps.label: The junction
steps.margin_note: Five wires meeting at one point: I₁, I₂ and I₃ enter, I₄ and I₅ leave.
steps.why: The arrows are the whole content of the junction rule. Which currents are added and which are subtracted is decided by the arrow directions, not by the numbering.
common_mistakes: Drawing the arrows without marking which way each current runs.

recall.must_convey: That a junction is drawn with three currents entering and two leaving.
accept: three currents in two currents out
reject: P by Q equals R by S

steps.memory_tip: Draw the arrows first; the signs in the equation follow them.

steps.label: Kirchhoff's voltage law
lines: Kirchhoff's second law (loop rule):
in any closed loop of a network the algebraic
sum of the potential differences is zero.
This law follows from the conservation of
energy.
For the single loop drawn below,

lines.text: ε − I R₁ − I R₂ − I R₃ = 0

steps.margin_note: Next two marks. Statement, Σ V = 0, the energy law, and one worked loop.
steps.why: Potential is a single-valued quantity, so going once round a loop and returning to the start must bring you back to the same potential. Each rise from the cell is matched by the drops across the resistors, which is conservation of energy for unit charge.
common_mistakes: Dropping the minus signs. A rise across the cell and a drop across a resistor have opposite signs.
Saying the loop rule follows from conservation of charge.

recall.must_convey: That the algebraic sum of potential differences round a closed loop is zero, and that this follows from conservation of energy.
accept: sum of potential differences in a closed loop is zero
reject: sum of currents at a junction is zero

steps.memory_tip: Round the loop and back to the start: the potential must come back to where it began.

steps.label: The loop
steps.margin_note: One cell and three resistors in a single loop; the arrow fixes the direction taken as positive.
steps.why: A single loop is the simplest case in which the loop rule can be applied, and it gives the series formula as a by-product.
common_mistakes: Leaving the loop without a marked current direction, which makes every sign a guess.

recall.must_convey: That a closed loop is drawn with a cell and three resistors and a marked current direction.
accept: draw a loop with a cell and three resistors
reject: sum of currents at a junction

steps.memory_tip: Pick a direction, mark it once, and keep to it all the way round.

steps.label: The Wheatstone bridge
steps.margin_note: Four arms P, Q, R, S between A, C, B, D, with the galvanometer G across CD. The cell and key go between A and B and are described in the next step.
steps.why: The four arms form two paths from A to B: one through C and one through D. The galvanometer compares the potentials at C and D, so it reads zero exactly when the two paths divide the potential in the same ratio.
common_mistakes: Placing the galvanometer between A and B. It goes across CD, the other diagonal.

recall.must_convey: That the four arms P, Q, R and S are drawn between A, C, B and D with the galvanometer across CD.
accept: draw the bridge with four arms
P Q R S on the four arms
reject: P by Q equals R by S

steps.memory_tip: Cell on one diagonal, galvanometer on the other.

steps.label: The bridge equations
lines: A cell of emf ε with a key is joined between
A and B. Let the currents be i₁ in P, i₂ in R,
i₃ in Q, i₄ in S, and i₅ in the galvanometer
of resistance G.
Junction rule at C and at D:
Loop rule for the closed mesh ACDA:
Loop rule for the closed mesh CBDC:
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Name every current first, then write the four equations with their numbers.
steps.why: Two junctions and two meshes give four independent equations, which is exactly what is needed to eliminate the currents and leave a relation between the four resistances alone.
common_mistakes: Naming fewer than five currents, so one branch is left out.
Taking the galvanometer branch round both meshes with the same sign.

recall.must_convey: That the junction rule is applied at C and D and the loop rule to the meshes ACDA and CBDC.
accept: apply junction rule at C and D
apply loop rule to A C D A and C B D C
reject: P by Q equals R by S

steps.memory_tip: Two junctions, two meshes, four equations.

steps.label: The balance condition
lines: The bridge is balanced when the galvanometer
shows no deflection, that is when no current
passes through it:
Then (1) and (2) give i₁ = i₃ and i₂ = i₄,
and (3) and (4) become
Dividing (5) by (6),
This is the balancing condition of the
Wheatstone bridge.
steps.margin_note: Last two marks. Set i₅ = 0, divide the two mesh equations, and box P/Q = R/S.
steps.why: With i₅ = 0 the pairs i₁ = i₃ and i₂ = i₄ let every current cancel in the division, and only the ratio of the resistances survives. That is why the bridge measures an unknown resistance without needing to know the current or the emf.
common_mistakes: Writing P/R = Q/S. Both forms are true, but the asked form pairs the arms as P with Q and R with S.
Saying the galvanometer current is small at balance. It is exactly zero.

recall.must_convey: That putting the galvanometer current equal to zero and dividing the two mesh equations gives P by Q equals R by S.
accept: P by Q equals R by S
i five is zero at balance
reject: apply junction rule at C and D
heard_as: P by Q equals R by S

steps.memory_tip: Zero through the galvanometer, then divide: every current cancels and only P/Q = R/S is left.

insider_note: Two marks of this answer are the two conservation laws by name — charge for the junction rule, energy for the loop rule. Students who write only the equations lose them.
